Rc<Node> matches this single-threaded shared-ownership requirement.

writing.exampleCaption: Rc shares ownership on one thread. Arc also shares ownership, but uses atomic counts and only crosses threads when its inner bounds permit it.
writing.explanation:
`Box` has exactly one owner and puts the value on the heap. `Rc` shares ownership on a single thread with a plain count. `Arc` does the same across threads with an atomic count, which costs more. Choosing the narrowest one that fits is the whole answer.

All three can place data behind a pointer, but they solve different ownership problems. `Box<T>` owns one heap allocation and is useful for recursive structures, large values, or a stable sized pointer to a trait object. `Rc<T>` lets several owners on one thread share one allocation through a non-atomic count. `Arc<T>` uses an atomic count for ownership shared across threads when the inner type permits it. Neither `Rc` nor `Arc` automatically grants mutable access to the shared value.

Use a concrete data flow: one parser builds a tree and hands it to one consumer, so `Box` may be enough. Several UI nodes on one thread need a shared immutable model, so `Rc` can be appropriate. Workers on different threads read the same configuration, so `Arc` fits. If they edit shared state, add a mutex, channel, or another synchronization design. `Rc<RefCell<T>>` provides runtime borrow checking on one thread, not cross-thread safety.

A strong answer includes costs and failure modes. Reference counting updates on clone and drop; `Arc` uses atomic operations, but that does not guarantee it is meaningfully slower in every application. Cycles of strong `Rc` or `Arc` links can leak; use `Weak` for back-references. Ask who should own the value and for how long before choosing a pointer. The simplest ownership model that expresses the required lifetime is usually easier to maintain.

Before reaching for `Arc`, ask if ownership can be transferred to one worker instead. Fewer shared owners simplify shutdown and error handling.

Interview follow-up: Draw a strong reference cycle and replace a back-reference with Weak. Why does memory safety allow a leak?
